sources.news_title: Japan mall rebuilt after deadly 2016 earthquake destroyed in major temblor weeks after 'fresh start' reopening
sources.text:
A shopping mall in southern Japan that had just reopened after years of reconstruction following a devastating 2016 earthquake was destroyed Tuesday after a powerful earthquake struck the region and was followed by a massive explosion, leaving dozens of workers unaccounted for.
The Aeon Mall in Kumamoto Prefecture celebrated its grand reopening on June 13 after years of rebuilding meant to mark the region's recovery from the 2016 disaster.
Just weeks later, a magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck near Kumamoto, according to FOX Weather, citing the U.S. Geological Survey. Japan's Meteorological Agency measured the same quake at magnitude 7.1 using its own seismic scale.
EARTHQUAKE SHAKES PERU'S ANDES REGION, KILLING AT LEAST 5, DISPLACING HUNDREDS
About 200 shoppers were safely evacuated after the earthquake, officials said. Roughly an hour later, a powerful explosion ripped through the building, blowing off exterior walls and exposing its steel framework. NHK reported that about 20 to 30 mall employees remained unaccounted for, while police said rescuers could not immediately enter because of the risk of aftershocks.
The mall had become one of the most visible symbols of Kumamoto's recovery after the magnitude 7.3 earthquake that devastated the region in April 2016. Aeon said the redevelopment included seismic reinforcements and other safety improvements designed to make the complex more resilient.
Witnesses reported smelling gas before the explosion, according to Reuters. An Aeon spokesperson said employees immediately helped evacuate visitors after the quake, while prefectural officials confirmed about 200 people were guided safely outside before the blast.
EXCLUSIVE: FRANKLIN GRAHAM VISITS EMERGENCY HOSPITAL TREATING VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS
According to FOX Weather, the earthquake struck just before 4:30 p.m. local time about 9 miles north of Kumamoto at a depth of roughly 6 miles. Japan's Meteorological Agency briefly issued and later lifted a tsunami advisory for parts of Kyushu. NHK reported at least 50 people were injured, while Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency said the quake sparked at least eight fires. Kumamoto Airport also temporarily closed.
Reuters reported the mall welcomed more than 8 million visitors annually after Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. opened a factory nearby in 2024.
The complex housed about 200 stores, a movie theater and parking for roughly 5,000 vehicles. It also became known locally after a supermarket inside sold 10-yen onigiri to help survivors following the 2016 earthquake.

When the mall reopened in June, Aeon described the project as a "'re-start' initiative" marking both the shopping center's 21st anniversary and the region's recovery from the 2016 earthquake.
As night fell Tuesday, rescue operations remained on hold because of continuing aftershocks as families awaited word on the employees still believed to be inside.

sources.text:
Politics
Major Earthquake Rocks Southern Japan
A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday, causing widespread damage across the island of Kyushu, leaving dozens of people injured or missing, disrupting transportation and power, and prompting a tsunami advisory that was later lifted. Rescue crews continue searching for survivors as authorities assess the full extent of the destruction.
The earthquake struck near Kumamoto Prefecture at approximately 4:27 p.m. local time, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. The epicenter was located about 20 kilometers south of Kumamoto City, a region still remembered for the devastating earthquakes that struck the area in 2016. The quake was felt across much of southern Japan and caused buildings to shake violently, roads to crack, and transportation systems to grind to a halt.
One of the hardest-hit locations was an Aeon shopping mall in Kashima Town, where a large explosion occurred shortly after the earthquake. Officials believe the blast may have been caused by a gas leak, although investigators have not yet confirmed the exact cause.
Part of the mall collapsed, trapping numerous workers and prompting a massive search-and-rescue operation involving firefighters, police, and military personnel. Authorities said between 20 and 30 workers were initially unaccounted for, while multiple people were feared dead.
WATCH: The moment an explosion occurred at Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, Japan, following a powerful earthquake. pic.twitter.com/mIA5x23sGc
— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) July 28, 2026
Additional damage was reported at a Nippon Paper Industries facility, where a large chimney collapsed, leaving several workers trapped beneath the rubble.
Hospitals across the region treated dozens of injured residents, including people hurt by falling debris, collapsing buildings, and transportation accidents that occurred during the quake. More than 50 injuries had been reported by Tuesday evening, though officials warned those numbers could rise as rescue operations continued per Reuters.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said emergency officials were still determining the full scope of the disaster but confirmed that fires, power outages, damaged bridges, and collapsed structures had been reported across the region.
The government quickly mobilized hundreds of members of Japan’s Self-Defense Forces to assist with rescue efforts while urging residents to evacuate vulnerable areas and prepare for additional aftershocks. Approximately 300,000 people were advised or ordered to move to evacuation centers as a precaution.
BREAKING: A powerful magnitude 7.1 earthquake has struck near Kumamoto, Japan. pic.twitter.com/hapnsKS5bP
— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) July 28, 2026
The quake also disrupted critical infrastructure throughout Kyushu. Nearly 50,000 homes temporarily lost electricity, while mobile phone networks experienced outages due to damaged transmission equipment.
Rail operators suspended Shinkansen bullet train service, flights at Kumamoto Airport were halted, and several major highways suffered significant cracking that left traffic at a standstill. Major manufacturers including Sony, Honda, Fujifilm, Tokyo Electron, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. temporarily suspended or reduced operations while facilities were inspected for damage.
Officials initially issued a tsunami advisory for portions of the Ariake and Yatsushiro Seas immediately after the earthquake. The advisory prompted coastal residents to seek higher ground before it was lifted several hours later after authorities determined the threat had diminished. Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority also confirmed there were no abnormalities at nearby nuclear power plants following inspections.
A 6.8 magnitude earthquake in Japan has left people trapped in a shopping mall and several people are unaccounted for at a paper factory.
The number of dead and injured is unclear at this time. pic.twitter.com/Ja6S3ngtdD
— Kentucky Girl (@Notwokenow) July 28, 2026
Japan sits along the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” one of the world’s most active seismic zones, making earthquakes a frequent occurrence. Kumamoto itself experienced a catastrophic series of earthquakes in 2016 that killed hundreds of people and severely damaged historic landmarks, including Kumamoto Castle. Tuesday’s earthquake caused additional damage to portions of the castle that had only recently undergone years of restoration.
The Japan Meteorological Agency warned residents that strong aftershocks could continue for at least the next week, increasing the risk of landslides and further structural collapses. Emergency crews remained on scene late Tuesday, racing against time to locate survivors trapped beneath collapsed buildings as authorities continued to evaluate one of Japan’s strongest earthquakes of the year.

sources.news_title: Workers missing after Japanese quake and mall blast
sources.text:
Workers missing after Japanese quake and mall blast
A 7.1-magnitude earthquake has hit Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture, knocking out power to thousands of homes, rupturing roads and leaving some trapped and others presumed dead inside a partially collapsed shopping mall.
Speaking to reporters from her office in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago.
"We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings," Takaichi said.
"I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location."
About 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, and hundreds of soldiers have been deployed to help with rescue operations as aftershocks continued to rumble in the area, on Japan's southwestern island of Kyushu.
About 20 to 30 workers at the prefecture's largest shopping mall were unaccounted for after it was rocked by an explosion in the aftermath of the quake, NHK said.
Fire services earlier said several people were trapped inside.
Local news outlets quoted police saying several had died or were presumed to have perished in the incident, although Reuters could not immediately confirm the reports.
One side of the mall, which houses about 200 stores, was torn away, exposing steel beams and strewing debris across a vast parking lot, footage showed.
Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside as rescue teams searched for survivors.
A spokesperson for mall operator Aeon said customers and employees were led out right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear.
Authorities are investigating a possible gas explosion, broadcaster NTV reported.
Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he was stunned by the blast while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall.
"It was a huge impact," he said.
"A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling."
Multiple people were also unaccounted for after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, broadcaster NHK reported, while two hospitals were each reported to be treating more than 50 people, some in serious condition.
Several passengers aboard high-speed trains at the time of the quake were also injured, operators said.
Authorities said they were responding to multiple incidents where buildings had partially collapsed or had caught fire.
One person died in one such collapse in a town near the epicentre, TV Asahi reported.
Some roads were also badly damaged, with large cracks splintering major highways, snarling traffic.
Rail services were suspended and flights grounded.
The quake's epicentre was 20km south of Kumamoto city, central Kyushu's largest city with a population of about 700,000.
Residents in the areas that felt the biggest tremors must be on alert for further strong quakes for about a week, as well as for the risk of landslides, an official for the Japan Meteorological Agency said.
About 100 small aftershocks have hit Kumamoto already since the initial jolt, JMA said.
With thousands of homes still without power as night fell, authorities warned residents about the risk of heat stroke as temperatures were set to hit 34C on Wednesday.

sources.news_title: Southern Japan earthquake traps people in collapsed shopping mall
sources.text:
Rescue teams searched through a damaged shopping centre and an industrial site in southern Japan on Tuesday after a major earthquake struck Kumamoto prefecture, leaving people missing, injuring dozens and forcing about 300,000 residents towards evacuation centres.
The tremor hit inland on Kyushu island at 4.27pm local time, close to the city of Uki and about 20 kilometres south of Kumamoto city.
Japan’s meteorological authorities initially measured the earthquake at magnitude 7.1. The US Geological Survey later revised its estimate to 6.8. The epicentre was shallow, at about 10 kilometres below ground, increasing the force of the shaking across nearby communities.
Emergency crews focused on Aeon Mall Kumamoto in Kashima Town after an explosion followed the initial tremor. Footage showed part of the building torn open, with steel beams exposed and debris spread across the car park.
Japan’s public broadcaster NHK reported that between 20 and 30 workers remained unaccounted for. Fire officials said the second floor had collapsed and that several people were trapped inside.
Japanese broadcasters TBS, TV Asahi and Fuji TV reported that several people had died or were presumed dead at the mall.
A senior government official told Japanese reporters that the mall had reported a gas leak, according to NHK. The official said workers had shut the main gas valve while police, fire crews and the Self-Defense Forces continued rescue operations. Aeon said the cause of the explosion remained under investigation.
An Aeon spokesperson said staff had evacuated customers and employees after the earthquake and before the blast.
The earthquake damaged roads, bridges and buildings across Kumamoto.
A train derailed at Yatsushiro station, injuring several passengers. JR Kyushu suspended rail services, while Kumamoto Airport closed its runway and airlines cancelled or diverted flights.
About 48,000 homes lost power, and some mobile services were disrupted.
Hospitals across the region treated scores of injured people. NHK said one hospital received more than 50 patients, while another treated about 40 people, including 10 in serious condition.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the government was still assessing the scale of the disaster.
“We have already been informed that people have been injured,” Takaichi told reporters in Tokyo. “Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings.”
She urged residents to move to safe locations and remain alert for another earthquake of similar strength.
Takaichi said 3,600 soldiers would support rescue and recovery work. Fire services, police, coast guard units and local emergency teams also joined the response.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara asked residents in the areas with the strongest shaking to follow local evacuation orders and official information.
About 300,000 people received instructions to move to shelters as aftershocks continued across Kumamoto. The Japan Meteorological Agency recorded about 100 smaller tremors after the main earthquake.
The agency warned that residents in the worst-hit areas face the risk of further strong earthquakes for about a week. Officials also warned of landslides in areas where the shaking had weakened slopes and roads.
A tsunami warning issued after the earthquake was lifted within about an hour.
Kumamoto Castle, one of the region’s main cultural sites, also sustained damage. Officials said parts of its stone walls collapsed during the earthquake. The castle closed for the day and asked visitors to place their safety first.
The site was still undergoing repairs following the earthquakes that struck Kumamoto in 2016.
Japan lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, where several tectonic plates meet. The country records about 1,500 earthquakes each year and accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s earthquakes at magnitude 6 or above.
Authorities also warned residents without electricity about the risk of heatstroke. Temperatures in Kumamoto were forecast to reach about 34°C on Wednesday.

sources.news_title: Japan 7.1 quake: Many feared trapped in mall
sources.text:
“Many people” were feared trapped in a stricken shopping mall in Japan late yesterday, authorities said, after a major earthquake toppled buildings, sparked fires and reportedly injured more than 100 people.
In Taipei, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said that no Taiwanese nationals had been reported injured or otherwise affected by the quake.
Japanese private broadcaster TBS reported that a “considerable number” were feared dead inside the mall in the town of Kashima after the fire brigade said that the second floor collapsed in the magnitude 7.1 tremor.
Photo: Kyodo News via AP
Public broadcaster NHK cited police sources as saying that between 20 and 30 employees could not be contacted, showing footage of emergency vehicles with flashing red lights outside.
Police said they could not confirm any fatalities inside the building. Kyodo News reported that four people had been taken to hospital, all of them conscious.
Multiple people were also believed to be unaccounted for at a Japan Paper Industries factory where the tip of a chimney fell down, NHK reported, citing sources.
One person was killed when a house collapsed during the quake, Kyodo reported.
Footage elsewhere in the southwestern Kumamoto region on the island of Kyushu aired by NHK earlier showed several blazes, damaged bridges, a derailed cargo train and a number of houses threatening to topple over.
The quake at 4:27pm had a magnitude of 7.1, the Japan Meteorological Agency said, but reached the highest level of seven on Japan’s Shindo scale of shaking. A succession of aftershocks followed, including one with a magnitude of 6.1 at 5:08pm.
The US Geological Survey determined the magnitude of the quake at 6.8.
MOFA said its representative office in Fukuoka, which is responsible for consular affairs in Kumamoto Prefecture, immediately contacted Taiwanese nationals known to be in the affected area.
All those contacted reported they were safe, and the office had not received any requests for emergency assistance from Taiwanese citizens in Kumamoto.
MOFA urged Taiwanese in Kumamoto who require assistance to contact the Fukuoka office’s emergency hotline at +81-90-1922-9740.
The ministry also said it had informed the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association’s Taipei office that Taiwan stood ready to assist Japan with post-disaster relief efforts.
Many roads were closed and high-speed Shinkansen train services were suspended in the region. Kumamoto airport was closed before being re-opened last night.
Two hospitals reported taking in at least 50 injured patients each, NHK said.
“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” NHK quoted an employee at one hospital as saying.
“Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures,” the employee said.
The broadcaster also said that about 10 people were hurt at a nursing home for the elderly.
“We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries,” Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said.
“Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed,” she said.
The Japanese military has mobilized 3,600 personnel for disaster relief operations and sent 20 aircraft to assess the damage from the air, the minister of defense said.
The Japan Meteorological Agency initially issued an alert for a possible tsunami of up to 1m, but withdrew the warning at about 6:10pm.
Unverified footage shared on social media showed parts of a wall at the centuries-old Kumamoto Castle collapsing.
No immediate abnormalities were recorded at nuclear power plants, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.
About 45,000 households and facilities had no power in the Kumamoto region, local utility Kyushu Electric Power said.
The firm said three nuclear reactors operating in the region at the time were functioning normally.
A local NHK staffer wearing a helmet reported live on air that the shaking was continuing about half an hour after the quake, with the newsroom rocking so violently that it was difficult to remain standing.
“Including myself, there may be some people who feel their hearts racing,” the staffer said.
Kumamoto was hit by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 — one of magnitude 6.5, followed two days later by one of magnitude 7.3 — which killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.
Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive magnitude 9.0 undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing about 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear power plant.

sources.news_title: Powerful 7.1-Magnitude Earthquake Rocks Southern Japan — Crisis Deepens After The Shaking Stops – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Jack
sources.text:
Southern Japan was still counting the damage from a massive earthquake when a second emergency erupted.
The first shock struck the Kumamoto region late Tuesday afternoon, snapping roads, damaging buildings, starting fires and throwing parts of Kyushu into darkness.
Then, after the shaking had stopped and an evacuation was underway, an explosion tore through one of the prefecture’s largest shopping malls.
Rescue crews were searching the wreckage Tuesday night as workers remained unaccounted for and police warned that lives may have been lost.
NHK WORLD’s first aerial look showed just how widespread the emergency response had become:
The Japan Meteorological Agency placed the quake at 4:27 p.m. local time on July 28. Its epicenter was in the Kumamoto region at a shallow depth of roughly 10 kilometers, or about six miles.
JMA gave the earthquake a magnitude of 7.1 and recorded a maximum seismic intensity of 7 in Uki City and Hikawa Town. That is the highest point on Japan’s shindo scale, which measures the strength of shaking at a particular location rather than the total energy released by the quake.
Strong shaking spread well beyond the epicenter. Kumamoto’s southern ward registered an upper 6, while multiple communities across Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga and Miyazaki reached levels capable of causing major damage.
The agency issued a tsunami advisory for the Ariake and Yatsushiro Seas, then lifted it within two hours. No tsunami was observed from the inland quake.
The U.S. Geological Survey reviewed the same event at magnitude 6.8, centered about three miles east of Uto at a depth of 10 kilometers. JMA’s detailed mechanism page also lists a moment magnitude of 6.8 alongside its domestic magnitude of 7.1.
Those figures describe the quake through different measurement methods. They do not change what people on the ground experienced: the most severe level of shaking Japan’s intensity scale can record.
USGS placed the event on its highest alert tier for likely economic losses. Its current ShakeMap concentrates the strongest modeled shaking around Uto, Uki and the southern side of Kumamoto.
The reviewed location sits close to heavily populated communities and major transportation routes.
Japan’s government moved quickly from assessment to emergency response.
The Prime Minister’s Office of Japan said Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had received reports of injuries, power outages and fires, along with damaged roads and bridges and collapsed buildings. She said the government had created an emergency task force and was putting lives first.
Thousands of military personnel were being deployed to assist rescue operations while aircraft surveyed the hardest-hit areas. The government told agencies to collect damage information immediately, coordinate with local authorities and put rescue work ahead of everything else.
Authorities also warned residents to stay away from damaged structures and prepare for more strong shaking. Rail service across Kyushu was halted for inspections, flights were grounded and sections of highway cracked or shifted.
The earthquake itself was only part of the crisis.
Reuters reported that an explosion rocked Aeon Mall Kumamoto after customers and employees had begun evacuating following the initial quake. One side of the roughly 200-store complex was ripped open, exposing steel beams and scattering debris across the parking lot.
Fire officials said multiple people were trapped. NHK reported that roughly 20 to 30 workers were unaccounted for, while police told TBS that fatalities were feared.
The exact cause of the blast was still unknown. The explosion happened in the quake’s aftermath, but officials had not established that the earthquake directly caused it.
Hospitals were also treating scores of injured people. Reuters cited NHK reports that one hospital had received more than 50 patients and another about 40, including 10 people in serious condition.
Video from inside the region captured the violent side-to-side motion as it happened:
WATCH: Powerful shaking sends a building swaying side to side after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Kumamoto, Japan pic.twitter.com/NYeGx7ZCSS
— Insider Paper (@TheInsiderPaper) July 28, 2026
Kumamoto City reported that 181 shelters were open by 9 p.m. local time, housing 1,512 people from 858 households. Officials had ordered every city shelter opened as the damage assessment continued into the night.
Power was out at more than 47,000 homes across the prefecture at that hour. Parts of the city also lost gas and water service, while emergency crews responded to fires, people trapped in elevators and a road crack that forced a closure near the Midorikawa River.
The city applied Japan’s Disaster Relief Act across 21 municipalities because large numbers of people had been injured or faced an immediate threat to life and safety.
Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority reported no abnormalities at three nearby nuclear power plants, removing one of the most feared possibilities from the early damage picture.
Kumamoto knows how dangerous the next phase can be.
A devastating earthquake sequence struck the same region in 2016. The larger shock arrived after an earlier major quake, a history Japanese officials invoked as they warned people not to assume the danger had passed.
The first hours brought maximum-level shaking, widespread infrastructure damage, fires, blackouts, injuries and a mass evacuation.
What followed at the mall turned an already serious disaster into a race against time.
For the families waiting on word from rescue crews, the earthquake may have ended in seconds. The emergency did not.

sources.news_title: Powerful quake hits southern Japan, shopping mall explosion leaves some trapped and others presumed dead
sources.text: TOKYO — A 7.1 magnitude earthquake shook Japan ‘s southern main island of Kyushu on Tuesday, leaving dozens of people injured or missing after part of a shopping centre and a huge chimney at a paper factory collapsed, officials said. A tsunami advisory was issued but quickly lifted. There were fears that at least two people were dead. In Kashima Town, the quake collapsed the second floor of the Aeon Mall shopping centre, trapping an unknown number of people there, according to the fire department in the prefectural capital of Kumamoto. Japan’s NHK national television said the collapse came after an explosion, believed to have been triggered by a gas leak at the building. Four people were pulled out with injuries and taken to a hospital, while 10 others were unaccounted for, the Kumamoto prefectural emergency response team said. It said the extent of the damage was still being investigated as the search and rescue effort continued. At the Nippon Paper Industries Co.’s Yatsushiro factory, where a chimney collapsed and the building was damaged, 11 people were trapped underneath the debris, the Kumamoto emergency team said. Two of them were later found without vital signs, while the conditions of nine others were unknown, the team said. sources.news_title: 20 to 30 Workers Unaccounted for After Explosion Partially Collapses Japan Mall
sources.text:
A powerful earthquake struck Japan’s Kyushu island on Tuesday, 28 July, before an apparent explosion caused part of a major shopping mall to collapse.
The incident happened at Aeon Mall Kumamoto in Kashima town, close to the earthquake’s epicentre.
As of about 10:40pm Japan time (9:40pm Singapore time) on Tuesday, rescue operations were still under way. Around 20 to 30 mall workers could not be contacted, while the exact number of people trapped or killed remained unclear.
The Earthquake Struck at 4:27pm
The earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture at 4:27pm local time.
The Japan Meteorological Agency recorded a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 and a depth of around 10km. The quake reached shindo 7, the highest level on Japan’s seismic intensity scale, in parts of Kumamoto.
Unlike magnitude, which measures the energy released by an earthquake, the shindo scale measures how strongly the ground shakes at a particular location.
The United States Geological Survey initially assessed the earthquake at magnitude 7.1 before revising its estimate to 6.8.
An Explosion Happened More Than an Hour Later
Aeon said customers and employees began evacuating immediately after the earthquake.
However, more than an hour later, an apparent explosion struck the mall. Police and firefighters received reports of a loud explosion-like sound and smoke rising from the building.
The local fire department said part of the mall’s second floor collapsed, leaving an unknown number of people trapped inside. Aeon said the cause of the explosion had not been determined.
Claims circulating online that the explosion was caused by a damaged gas pipe have not been confirmed by Aeon, the police or fire authorities.
One Side of the Mall Was Torn Open
Aerial footage showed extensive damage to one side of the mall.
Parts of its exterior walls had been blown or torn away, exposing steel beams and the building’s interior. Large pieces of debris were scattered across the mall’s outdoor car park.
Emergency vehicles, including ambulances and fire engines, gathered outside as rescue workers entered the damaged building.
A man working at a pub about 300m away told Japanese broadcaster TBS that the explosion produced a large cloud of smoke and dust. He said the wind carried the dust towards the surrounding area, making it appear as though volcanic ash was falling.
Four People Were Taken to Hospital
At 10:06pm Japan time, TBS reported that four people had been taken from the mall to a nearby hospital.
Earlier reports said multiple people were trapped, while NHK reported that around 20 to 30 mall workers could not be reached.
The mall’s total workforce is much larger. Aeon’s published facility information from 2024 listed approximately 2,700 employees, including around 360 working at the main Aeon store. This does not mean all of them were working when the earthquake struck.
Reports About the Death Toll Remain Conflicting
Japanese news outlets issued conflicting reports about casualties at the mall during the first few hours of the rescue operation.
The Straits Times, citing Fuji TV, reported that multiple deaths had been confirmed. TBS reported that police and Kumamoto prefectural sources believed many people had died.
However, Kumamoto police subsequently told AFP that they could not confirm whether there had been any deaths at the mall.
Therefore, as of about 10:40pm Japan time on 28 July, the safest verified position was that several people were missing or trapped, four had been taken to hospital, and authorities had not released a consolidated official death toll for the mall.
The Japan Self-Defense Forces Are Helping With the Rescue
Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force personnel were deployed to help rescue those trapped inside Aeon Mall Kumamoto.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said 3,600 Self-Defense Forces personnel would be sent to the affected region as authorities dealt with collapsed buildings, fires, damaged roads and power outages.
Rescuers also faced the danger of further tremors. The Japan Meteorological Agency warned people in heavily shaken areas to remain alert for strong aftershocks, particularly over the following two to three days.
Aeon Mall Kumamoto Is One of the Prefecture’s Largest Malls
Aeon Mall Kumamoto is located in Kashima town, around 20km south of Kumamoto city.
The two-storey reinforced-concrete complex opened in October 2005 and was expanded in July 2018.
According to Aeon, it has around 200 speciality shops, approximately 120,000 sq m of total floor space and parking for about 5,000 vehicles. Its tenants include shops, restaurants, a food court, a cinema and the main Aeon retail store.
The mall had also been affected by the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes and was temporarily closed following that disaster. Aeon later expanded and renovated the complex.
Several Important Questions Are Still Unanswered
Authorities have not established what caused the explosion or whether it was directly triggered by earthquake damage.
It is also unclear how many workers or customers remained inside when the blast occurred, whether everyone reported missing was actually inside the building, and which part of the mall the explosion began in.
Structural investigators will also need to determine whether the second-floor collapse was caused by the explosion alone, damage from the earthquake, or a combination of both.
Until authorities complete the rescue operation and account for those missing, casualty figures from the mall are likely to change.

sources.text:
Stone walls at Kumamoto Castle were damaged during the violent shaking, according to Kyodo News. The landmark, one of Japan’s best-known castles, had already suffered extensive destruction during the deadly Kumamoto earthquakes of 2016 and undergone years of restoration work.
Tuesday’s earthquake was initially measured at magnitude 7.1 by the U.S. Geological Survey, which later revised its estimate to 6.8. Japanese authorities issued a tsunami advisory shortly after the quake, although it was lifted within two hours after no tsunami was observed.
Kumamoto earthquake damages historic castle

Earthquake in Japan injures 40
Authorities were still working to establish the number of casualties, but Kyodo reported that a hospital in Yatsushiro city had received around 40 people injured in the earthquake.A train derailed at Yatsushiro station and fell onto its side, according to the news agency.
Emergency services also received numerous calls reporting fires and damage to homes.
In Mashiki, Yozo Kai, a priest at a Shinto shrine, said several stone lanterns toppled during the quake. He feared the shaking could once again damage the shrine’s main hall and gate.
Japan news: Tsunami advisory issued, later lifted

Japan’s Defense Ministry dispatched aircraft to survey the affected region and assess damage from above.

The latest earthquake struck a region that still carries scars from the devastating Kumamoto earthquakes of April 2016.More than 50 people were killed and around 1,800 injured in that disaster, while tens of thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed.
Kumamoto Castle became one of the most visible symbols of the destruction after its centuries-old stone walls collapsed in several places.

A Sony spokesman earlier said it was checking the situation.

sources.news_title: 'Considerable' number of people feared dead in Japan mall after quake
sources.text:
A major earthquake collapsed buildings and sparked fires in Japan's southwest.
Image: Jiji Press / AFP
A "considerable number" of people have reportedly died in a shopping mall damaged by a major earthquake in southwestern Japan on Tuesday, broadcaster TBS said.
Earlier police told AFP that they could not confirm whether there were any fatalities at the mall in the town of Kashima.
Emergency services earlier said that "many people" were trapped inside the building after a floor collapsed.
In "Kashima town, a shopping complex's second floor collapsed, leaving many people trapped inside," the fire department said in a statement.
Police said earlier they had received reports of what sounded like an explosion at the Aeon Mall outlet in the Kumamoto region.
Collapsed buildings and fires
The major earthquake collapsed buildings and sparked fires in Japan's southwest, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Tuesday, with broadcaster NHK saying that at least 50 people were taken to hospital.
Television footage on NHK showed several blazes, damaged bridges, a derailed cargo train and cracked roads after the tremor on Kyushu island. The broadcaster reported at least 12 collapsed houses.
The quake at 4:27pm (local time) had a magnitude of 7.1, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency, but reached the highest possible level of seven on Japan's Shindo scale of shaking.
The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake -- one of hundreds that strike Japan every year - at 6.8. The vast majority cause little damage.
"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Takaichi said.
"Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed," she said.
The JMA initially issued an alert for a possible tsunami of up to one metre (three feet), but withdrew the warning at around 6:10pm.
"This earthquake occurred inland, and no tsunami activity has been observed so far. For this reason, we hope to lift the tsunami advisory at a relatively early stage, depending on future sea level conditions," a Japan Meteorological Agency spokesperson said.
No immediate abnormalities were recorded at nuclear power plants, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.
About 45,000 households and facilities have no power in the Kumamoto region, according to local utility Kyushu Electric Power.
The firm added that three nuclear reactors operating in the region at the time were functioning normally.
'Shaking is continuing'
A local NHK staffer wearing a helmet reported live on air that the shaking was continuing around half an hour after the quake, with the newsroom rocking so violently that it was difficult to remain standing.
"Shaking is continuing as I speak. Including myself, there may be some people who feel their hearts racing," the staffer said.
"When the quake struck, the shaking was so big that I could not stand up. Please be aware of the possibility that shaking might continue after this."
Kumamoto was hit by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 -- one of magnitude 6.5, followed two days later by one of magnitude 7.3 -- which killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.
A quake with a magnitude of 7.2 hit northern Japan on June 25 but caused no deaths or major damage.
Japan is one of the world's most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire".
The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18 percent of the world's earthquakes.
The vast majority are mild, although the damage they cause varies according to their location and the depth below the Earth's surface at which they strike.
Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.
A tremor measuring 7.7 hit the country's north on April 20 this year, injuring at least 10 people and shaking large buildings in Tokyo.
That prompted authorities to issue a special advisory warning of an increased risk of earthquakes of magnitude 8.0 or stronger.
The advisory was lifted after a week.
AFP

sources.news_title: 7.1 magnitude quake shakes Japan’s Kyushu and people are missing after a shopping center collapses - Boston News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
TOKYO (AP) — An earthquake registering a magnitude of 7.1 shook Japan’s southern main island of Kyushu and caused part of a shopping center to collapse on Tuesday, leaving dozens of people missing or injured, officials and reports said. A tsunami advisory was issued but quickly lifted.
The second floor of the Aeon Mall shopping center in Kashima Town collapsed, trapping an unknown number of people. Around 20 to 30 employees were missing while several other people were dug out and taken to a hospital, Kyodo News agency reported, quoting local police.
The affected area is about 900 kilometers (540 miles) southwest of Tokyo. A tsunami advisory for the Ariake and Yatsushiro Seas on the western coasts of Kumamoto prefecture and three neighboring prefectures was lifted within two hours, the Japan Meteorological Agency said.
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters there were reports of damage to roads, bridges and buildings, as well as blackouts and fires, though details were unclear.
Japan’s Fire and Disaster Management Agency said there were no reports of damage to major public facilities or infrastructure. Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority said no abnormalities were found at three nearby nuclear power plants.
Kyodo said a hospital in Yatsushiro city took in about 40 people with injuries and about 50 others were taken to a hospital in Kumamoto city.
Shinkansen bullet trains and local trains in Kyushu were suspended for safety checks, and the runway at Aso Kumamoto Airport was closed, with “no prospect of resuming operations,” according to a notice on the airport’s website. There were no details.
The Japanese Defense Ministry said it dispatched aircraft to the area to assess the situation.
A train derailed and fell on its side at Yatsushiro station, and stone walls were damaged at Kumamoto castle, Kyodo said.
“The shaking reminded me of the Kumamoto quake (10 years ago) and I was frightened,” said Hiroki Shimoda, an official at Mifune town hall, who saw roof tiles of nearby homes crash to the ground. Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead.
Shinji Kiyomoto with the Japan Meteorological Agency urged residents to be cautious over the next two to three days.

Major quake hits southern Japan, workers missing after mall blast
Tokyo ― A 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday, knocking out power to thousands of homes, rupturing roads and leaving some trapped and others presumed dead inside a partially collapsed shopping mall.
Speaking to reporters from her office in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago.
"We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings," Takaichi said.
"I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location."
Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centers, and hundreds of soldiers have been deployed to help with rescue operations as aftershocks continued to rumble in the area, on Japan's southwestern island of Kyushu.
'Like volcanic ash was falling'
Around 20 to 30 workers at the prefecture's largest shopping mall were unaccounted for after it was rocked by an explosion in the aftermath of the quake, NHK said.
Fire services earlier said multiple people were trapped inside.
Local news outlets quoted police saying several had died or were presumed to have perished in the incident, although Reuters could not immediately confirm the reports.
One side of the mall, which houses around 200 stores, was torn away, exposing steel beams and strewing debris across a vast parking lot, footage showed. Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside, as rescue teams searched for survivors.
A spokesperson for mall operator Aeon 8267.T said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear. Authorities are investigating a possible gas explosion, broadcaster NTV reported.
Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he was stunned by the blast while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall.
"It was a huge impact," he said. "A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling."
Multiple people were also unaccounted for after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, broadcaster NHK reported, while two hospitals were each reported to be treating more than 50 people, some in serious condition. Several passengers aboard high-speed trains at the time of the quake were also injured, operators said.
Buildings on fire
Authorities said they were responding to multiple incidents where buildings had partially collapsed or had caught fire. One person died in one such collapse in a town near the epicentre, TV Asahi reported.
Some roads were also badly damaged, with large cracks splintering major highways, snarling traffic. Rail services were suspended and flights grounded.
TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, Sony and Fujifilm evacuated workers from their plants following the quake. TSMC said in a statement late Tuesday that its site was unaffected and operations were gradually resuming.
However, Tokyo Electron, a semiconductor equipment maker, said it was suspending operations at its two factories in Kumamoto through Wednesday, while Honda said it would also temporarily idle its motorcycle factory there.
The quake’s epicentre was about 20 kilometres (12 miles) south of Kumamoto city, central Kyushu's largest city with a population of around 700,000.
Residents in the areas that felt the biggest tremors must be on alert for further strong quakes for about a week, as well as for the risk of landslides, an official for the Japan Meteorological Agency said. About 100 small aftershocks have hit Kumamoto already since the initial jolt, JMA said.
Tsunami warning lifted
Located along the "Ring of Fire" of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20% of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more.
A tsunami warning was issued immediately after Tuesday's quake, but was later lifted.
Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway, as airlines diverted and cancelled flights.
Telecoms operators KDDI and Docomo said there was disruption to their mobile phone services due to power shortages and transmission-line failures.
There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan's nuclear regulation authority said.
A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city's castle, a top tourist site.
Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of Tuesday's quake, an official at the castle's office said.
With thousands of homes still without power as night fell, authorities warned residents about the risk of heatstroke as temperatures were set to hit 34 degrees Celsius (93 degrees Fahrenheit) on Wednesday.

Two people killed in shopping mall collapse, Japanese public broadcaster NHK says
Two women in their 20s have died after a shopping mall in Japan partially collapsed in an explosion following Tuesday’s earthquake, according to the country’s public broadcaster NHK.
Six other people have so far been rescued from the site, including one who had suffered from a “cardiopulmonary arrest” and five who were hurt but do not have life-threatening injuries, NHK reported.
Earlier, CNN affiliate TV Asahi cited police sources as saying that several people had been killed in the mall collapse after a 6.8-magnitude earthquake struck the city of Kumamoto, in southern Japan.

NHK previously said 20 to 30 employees at Aeon Mall Kumamoto could not be contacted after the collapse.
This post has been updated with more details on the death toll.
3,600 military personnel mobilized to "expedite" rescue efforts in Japan
Thousands of military personnel have been mobilized in Japan amid an effort to “expedite” rescue and relief efforts, the country’s public broadcaster NHK reported Wednesday morning local time.
In response to a request from authorities in Kumamoto prefecture, where the 6.8-magnitude struck on Tuesday, NHK said defense forces had “mobilized approximately 3,600 personnel.”
The military personnel, who will work in coordination with local police and fire departments, will assess damage in order to “accelerate rescue and relief efforts,” NHK reported.

The factory sustained significant damage as a result of the 6.8-magnitude quake, with one of its chimneys snapping off, footage and images show.
Local officials said in an overnight briefing that two people were found in a “state of cardiopulmonary arrest” at the factory, NHK said, without confirming whether the two were alive or not. “The whereabouts of nine others remain unknown,” the public broadcaster added.
Japan quake sparks closure of more than 150 facilities in Kumamoto, local authorities say

As of early Wednesday morning local time, a total of 178 sites had been shut, including libraries, community centers, public parks and sports facilities, the city’s disaster prevention body posted on its website.

Here’s where the quake shook hardest:
Hospital in Kumamoto says it is "at full capacity" after earthquake

Adding to the pressure, the director said the hospital itself was damaged in the 6.8-magnitude quake, with water leaks and collapsed walls in several areas.
Four people rescued from Kumamoto shopping mall, authorities say
Four people have been rescued from Japan’s Aeon Mall Kumamoto, a shopping center which partially collapsed after today’s 6.8-magnitude earthquake, the country’s public broadcaster NHK said, citing local authorities.
However, NHK cited local officials as saying the whereabouts of at least 10 other people remains unknown.

What to know as rescue efforts continue after magnitude 6.8 quake hits Kumamoto
We’re tracking the latest developments after a deadly magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck Kumamoto prefecture in southern Japan on Tuesday.
A number of people were killed in the collapse at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, according to CNN affiliate TV Asahi, which cited police sources. They have not confirmed the number of deaths or whether those killed were employees or customers.

If you’re just joining us, here’s what else you need to know:
- Another earthquake, measuring magnitude 4.1, struck Kumamoto prefecture at 12:15 a.m. Wednesday local time, according to NHK One. No tsunami warning or threat was issued. Japan’s PM pledges full government response after powerful earthquake
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to support those affected by Tuesday’s powerful earthquake on the island of Kyushu, saying that her government will work tirelessly to respond to the emergency.
In a post on X, she expressed her “heartfelt sympathy to all those affected by this disaster,” adding that authorities would work “through the night” to determine the extent of the damage and coordinate emergency operations, including rescue work.
The earthquake poses another challenge for Takaichi, who has been in office for less than a year and has faced declining approval ratings in recent weeks amid public frustration over rising living costs and inflation.
Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, she said the government would put “human lives first” and respond with its “full force” to support communities affected by the disaster.
The government has pledged to provide essential supplies such as food and water, as well as portable air conditioners and power generators to help prevent heatstroke during Japan’s hot summer months.
Residents in areas that experienced the strongest shaking have been urged to remain vigilant, with authorities warning that aftershocks of similar strength could occur in the coming days.
Gas leak could have caused shopping mall explosion, officials say
Authorities believe the explosion at Japan’s Aeon Mall Kumamoto, a shopping center which partially collapsed after today’s earthquake, may have been caused by a gas leak, CNN affiliate TV Asahi reported.
The broadcaster cited multiple government officials as saying a strong smell of gas was detected at the scene.
One theory is that gas equipment used by restaurants in the mall could have been “damaged by the earthquake, causing a gas leak that later ignited and exploded,” TV Asahi said.
But investigations are ongoing to determine the exact cause of the explosion at the center, where many people remain trapped.
Dashcam footage shows a large emergency response at Aeon Mall Kumamoto
Footage posted on NHK One’s website shows a large presence of emergency crews at Aeon Mall Kumamoto.
Many people are trapped after the shopping mall partially collapsed. According to NHK One, “multiple people’s whereabouts (are) unknown.”
Earthquake rattled a region still reeling from 2016 disaster
The powerful 6.8-magnitude earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture rattled a region still marked by one of the country’s deadliest recent disasters.
In 2016, a series of devastating earthquakes killed 275 people and injured thousands more across the prefecture. The disaster also caused widespread devastation, with more than 200,000 homes affected and economic losses estimated at several trillion yen, making it one of Japan’s costliest natural disasters in recent decades.
Among the most visible symbols of the destruction was Kumamoto Castle, one of Japan’s most famous landmarks and a major tourist attraction. The centuries-old fortress suffered severe damage, with sections of its stone walls collapsing and parts of its structures badly affected. Restoration was expected to take decades.
Tuesday’s earthquake has now caused further damage to the historic site, dealing another blow to a landmark that was still recovering over a decade after the 2016 disaster.
A tremor every day: Japan is one of world's most quake-prone nations
Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, where minor tremors occur on average every five minutes, according to Reuters.
While most are too small to cause significant damage, the country remains haunted by memories of the devastating magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami that struck its northeast coast in March 2011. That disaster left around 18,500 people dead or missing and triggered the Fukushima nuclear crisis, the world’s worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl in 1986.
Since then, Japan has significantly strengthened its disaster preparedness. It’s invested billions of dollars in rebuilding the worst-hit areas, bolstering tsunami defences, strengthening building standards, expanding sophisticated earthquake and tsunami monitoring systems, and improving nationwide evacuation planning and drills.
Rail services disrupted and airport in Kumamoto closed after earthquake
Rail services have been greatly disrupted, and the airport in Kumamoto has canceled all flights for the rest of the day following the earthquake.
Flights are scheduled to resume on Wednesday but the airport, which hosts both international and domestic routes, urged passengers to check before they travel.
Services on several railway lines have been suspended for the rest of the day too.

Aerial footage shows burning buildings and an overturned train in Kumamoto

A closer look at the Kumamoto prefecture in southern Japan
Kumamoto is situated in southern Japan, about 55 miles (90 kilometers) east of Nagasaki.

More than 46,000 households without power after strong quake
More than 46,000 households in the area are currently without power after the earthquake, according to Kyushu Electric Power, though the number seems to be decreasing, indicating that some power is being restored.
The company says it has established an emergency response unit to help restore power.
However, the Sendai nuclear power station, which is situated about 100 kilometers (62 miles) from the earthquake’s epicenter, hasn’t sustained any damage, according to the UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency which cited information from Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority.
In 2011, another earthquake in Japan triggered the world’s second-worst nuclear accident when tsunami waves severely damaged the Fukushima nuclear power station.

At least one killed, several missing in Japan mall collapse after 7.1-magnitude earthquake
A powerful earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday, toppling buildings, igniting fires and leaving dozens feared trapped in a shopping mall, with at least one person reported dead and more than 100 injured. Emergency crews raced to rescue survivors as aftershocks rattled the region.

Dozens of people were feared trapped in a shopping mall in Japan on Tuesday after a major earthquake toppled buildings, sparked fires and reportedly killed one person and injured more than 100.
Private broadcaster TBS reported that a "considerable number" of people were feared dead inside the mall in the town of Kashima after the fire brigade said that the second floor collapsed in the 7.1-magnitude tremor.
Emergency services earlier said "many people" were trapped inside the building.
Public broadcaster NHK cited police sources as saying that between 20 and 30 employees could not be contacted, showing footage of emergency vehicles with flashing red lights outside.
Watch moreJapan hit by 7.1-magnitude earthquake
Police told AFP they could not confirm any fatalities inside the building. Kyodo News reported that four people had been taken to hospital, all of them conscious.
Multiple people were also believed to be unaccounted for at a factory in Yatsushiro city where the tip of a chimney fell down, NHK reported, citing sources.
One person was killed when a house collapsed during the quake, Kyodo reported.
NHK aired footage from elsewhere in the southwestern Kumamoto region on Kyushu island showing several blazes, damaged bridges, a derailed cargo train and a number of houses threatening to topple over.
Chiharu Hara, a 35-year-old recruitment agent who was in Kumamoto, told AFP that she was "terrified" when the quake struck.
"The office swayed violently side-to-side. I was afraid it would collapse. Everyone panicked," Hara said.
The tremor at 4:27pm (0727 GMT) had a magnitude of 7.1, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said, but reached the highest level of seven on Japan's Shindo scale.
The US Geological Survey put the magnitude at 6.8.
A succession of aftershocks followed, including one with a magnitude of 6.1 at 5:08pm.
Hundreds of earthquakes strike Japan every year, but the vast majority cause little damage.
Power outages, fires
Many roads were closed and high-speed shinkansen train services were suspended in the region affected by Tuesday's quake. Kumamoto airport was closed for several hours before re-opening in the evening.
Two hospitals reported taking in at least 50 injured patients each, NHK said.
"People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people," NHK quoted one hospital employee as saying.
"Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures."
The broadcaster also said that around 10 people were hurt at a nursing home for the elderly.
"Human casualties, building collapses, road damage, fires ... have been confirmed so far," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on X, adding there were also "water and power outages".
The Japanese military has mobilised 3,600 personnel for disaster relief operations and sent 20 aircraft to assess the damage from the air, the defence minister said.
The JMA initially issued a tsunami alert, but withdrew it at around 6:10pm.
Unverified footage shared on social media showed parts of a wall at the centuries-old Kumamoto Castle collapsing.

No immediate abnormalities were recorded at nuclear power plants, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.
About 45,000 households and facilities had no power in the Kumamoto region, according to local utility Kyushu Electric Power.
The firm said three nuclear reactors operating in the region at the time were functioning normally.
'Ring of Fire'
A local NHK staffer wearing a helmet reported live on air that the shaking was continuing around half an hour after the quake, with the newsroom rocking so violently that it was difficult to remain standing.
"Including myself, there may be some people who feel their hearts racing," the staffer said.
Kumamoto was hit by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 – one of magnitude 6.5, followed two days later by one of magnitude 7.3 – which killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.
Japan is one of the world's most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire".
The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18 percent of the world's earthquakes.
The vast majority are mild, although the damage they cause varies according to their location and the depth below the Earth's surface at which they strike.
Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters there were reports of damage to roads, bridges and buildings, as well as blackouts and fires, though details were unclear.
Japan’s Fire and Disaster Management Agency said there were no reports of damage to major public facilities or infrastructure. Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority said no abnormalities were found at three nearby nuclear power plants.
Kyodo said a hospital in Yatsushiro city took in about 40 people with injuries and about 50 others were taken to a hospital in Kumamoto city.
Shinkansen bullet trains and local trains in Kyushu were suspended for safety checks, and the runway at Aso Kumamoto Airport was closed, with “no prospect of resuming operations,” according to a notice on the airport’s website. There were no details.
The Japanese Defense Ministry said it dispatched aircraft to the area to assess the situation.
A train derailed and fell on its side at Yatsushiro station, and stone walls were damaged at Kumamoto castle, Kyodo said.
“The shaking reminded me of the Kumamoto quake (10 years ago) and I was frightened,” said Hiroki Shimoda, an official at Mifune town hall, who saw roof tiles of nearby homes crash to the ground. Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead.
Shinji Kiyomoto with the Japan Meteorological Agency urged residents to be cautious over the next two to three days.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

People trapped, deaths feared in mall explosion after Japan rocked by major earthquake
TOKYO — A 7.1-magnitude earthquake that hit Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday knocked out power to thousands of homes, ruptured roads and left some people trapped and others presumed dead inside a partially collapsed shopping mall.
Speaking to reporters at her office in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the number of casualties and extent of the damage in the area—which was devastated by a tremblor a decade ago—were still being assessed.
"We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings," Takaichi said.
"I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location."
'Like volcanic ash was falling'
One hospital had reported more than 50 injuries, public broadcaster NHK said. Several people on a high-speed train at the time of the quake were also injured, Nikkei newspaper said.
Multiple people were trapped inside an Aeon shopping mall rocked by an explosion that occurred after the earthquake, fire services said. Police said "quite a few" were presumed dead in the incident, broadcaster TBS reported.
An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear.
Kazuya Tsurunaga told broadcaster TBS he heard the explosion while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 meters from the Aeon mall.
"It was a huge impact," he said. "A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling."
Buildings on fire
Several other buildings were also on fire or partially collapsed, according to footage from NHK, while large cracks appeared on major roads, including an elevated highway. Rail services were halted and flights grounded.
TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, evacuated workers from its plant in the area as a precaution, a spokesperson for the firm said.
Sony and Fujifilm also evacuated staff from their plants in the area, Nikkei newspaper reported. A Sony spokesperson earlier said it was checking the situation.
Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centers, the disaster management agency said. The quake’s epicenter was about 20 kilometers south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island's largest city with a population of around 700,000.
Residents in the areas that felt the biggest tremors must beware of further strong quakes for about a week, as well as the risk of landslides, an official for the Japan Meteorological Agency said.
Tsunami warning lifted
Japan is one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes.
Located along the "Ring of Fire" of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20% of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more.
A tsunami warning was issued immediately after Tuesday's quake, but was later lifted.
Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway, as airlines diverted and cancelled flights.
Telecoms operators KDDI and Docomo said there was disruption to their mobile phone services due to power shortages and transmission-line failures.
There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan's nuclear regulation authority said.
A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city's castle, a top tourist site.
Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of Tuesday's quake, an official at the castle's office said. — Reuters

A 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture today, knocking out power to thousands of homes, rupturing roads and leaving some trapped and others presumed dead inside a partially collapsed shopping centre.
Speaking to reporters from her office in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago.
"We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings," Ms Takaichi said.
"I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location."
Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, and hundreds of soldiers have been deployed to help with rescue operations as aftershocks continued to rumble in the area, on Japan's southwestern island of Kyushu.
Around 20 to 30 workers at the prefecture's largest shopping centre were unaccounted for after it was rocked by an explosion in the aftermath of the earthquake, broadcaster NHK said.
Fire services earlier said multiple people were trapped inside.
Local news outlets quoted police saying several had died or were presumed to have perished in the incident, although Reuters could not immediately confirm the reports.
One side of the shopping centre, which houses around 200 stores, was torn away, exposing steel beams and strewing debris across a vast car park, footage showed. Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside, as rescue teams searched for survivors.
A spokesperson for the shopping centre operator Aeon said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial earthquake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear. Authorities are investigating a possible gas explosion, broadcaster NTV reported.

Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he was stunned by the blast while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon shopping centre.
"It was a huge impact," he said. "A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling."
Multiple people were also unaccounted for after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, broadcaster NHK reported, while two hospitals were each reported to be treating more than 50 people, some in serious condition. Several passengers aboard high-speed trains at the time of the quake were also injured, operators said.
Authorities said they were responding to multiple incidents where buildings had partially collapsed or had caught fire. One person died in one such collapse in a town near the epicentre, TV Asahi reported.
Some roads were also badly damaged, with large cracks splintering major motorways, snarling traffic. Rail services were suspended and flights grounded.
TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, Sony and Fujifilm evacuated workers from their plants following the quake. TSMC said in a statement this afternoon that its site was unaffected and operations were gradually resuming.
However, Tokyo Electron, a semiconductor equipment maker, said it was suspending operations at its two factories in Kumamoto through tomorrow, while Honda said it would also temporarily close its motorcycle factory there.
The quake's epicentre was about 20km (12 miles) south of Kumamoto city, central Kyushu's largest city with a population of around 700,000.
Residents in the areas that felt the biggest tremors must be on alert for further strong quakes for about a week, as well as for the risk of landslides, an official for the Japan Meteorological Agency said.
About 100 small aftershocks have hit Kumamoto already since the initial jolt, JMA said.
Located along the 'Ring of Fire' of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20% of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more.
A tsunami warning was issued immediately after today's earthquake, but was later lifted.

Telecoms operators KDDI and Docomo said there was disruption to their mobile phone services due to power shortages and transmission-line failures.
There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan's nuclear regulation authority said.
A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city's castle, a top tourist site.
Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of today's earthquake, an official at the castle's office said.
With thousands of homes still without power as night fell, authorities warned residents about the risk of heatstroke as temperatures are set to hit 34C tomorrow.

sources.news_title: Mall collapses in Japan after 7.1-magnitude earthquake with people trapped
sources.text:
A mall has partially collapsed leaving shoppers trapped inside after a large 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto in Japan on Tuesday.
Police say between 20 to 30 people are unaccounted for, according to Japanese public broadcaster NHK.
The earthquake, on Japan’s southern main island of Kyushu, hit in the afternoon and was followed by reports of an explosion at Aeon Mall Kumamoto in Kashima. Aerial photos showed the partially destroyed building, with the exterior wall no longer visible and framework exposed beneath.
Japan’s fire and disaster management agency has confirmed that the second floor of a "commercial facility" collapsed in the town, with multiple people trapped inside. Aeon told NHK that customers had been evacuated.
One hospital had reported more than 50 injuries, said NHK. Several people on a high-speed train at the time of the quake were also injured, Nikkei newspaper said. A train was derailed and fell on its side at the Yatsushiro station, Kyodo News agency reported.
Several people are missing after a chimney collapsed at the Nippon Paper Industries’ factory in the city of Yatsushiro, NHK reported. The fire and disaster management agency has said a rescue operation is underway.
All flights departing out of Aso Kumamoto Airport were canceled following the earthquake, according to a statement posted on the airport’s website. The airport said it plans to resume normal operations on Wednesday.
Despite the quake-related incidents, the fire and disaster management agency said there were no reports of damage to "critical" facilities and infrastructure, though authorities were still assessing the extent of damage.
Police told AFP that they were aware of reports of an explosion at the mall, but provided no further information. The Kyodo News agency reported that some of the people trapped inside the mall were injured, citing fire and rescue authorities.
Japan is frequently hit by earthquakes, suffering around 1,500 a year. Two separate earthquakes in Kumamoto in 2016 left at least 275 people dead, 2,739 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.
A video circulating on social media apparently filmed by someone in the mall’s parking lot in the aftermath of the earthquake shows people evacuating the building while smoke and dust can be seen around the building.
Warning After Earthquake Strikes
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on X that her government has set up a task force to gather information, assess possible damage and prepare for rescue operations if needed.
In remarks to reporters, Takaichi said the government would “spare no effort” in response measures, with the “highest priority placed on saving lives.”
She said there have been reports of a number of injuries and damage to roads, bridges and the collapse of buildings, as well as blackouts and fires. “I urge everyone to take immediate action to protect themselves, including by evacuating to a safe location,” she said.
Takaichi also warned people to be careful using fire or cooking appliances.
She added: “In areas that experienced strong tremors, earthquakes of similar intensity may continue to occur over approximately the next week. Please remain vigilant. The Government will continue to respond with every available resource.”
A tsunami advisory was temporarily issued but was lifted within two hours, the Japan Meteorological Agency said.
The agency said the tsunami advisory had covered the nearby Ariake and Yatsushiro Seas on the western coasts of Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Fukuoka and Saga prefectures.
Japan Meteorological Agency recorded the earthquake as 7.1-magnitude but the U.S. Geological Survey later revised it to 6.8.
The U.N. atomic watchdog has said that the earthquake did not cause any damage or safety issues to a nuclear power plant in the region.
The International Atomic Energy Agency wrote on X that it had been informed by Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority that the earthquake "caused no damage or safety issues at the Sendai Nuclear Power Plant, located around 100 km from the epicenter, and that it remains in operation." The watchdog said it would "continue to monitor the situation."
The power of the quake was illustrated by a picture showing the collapse of the walls surrounding Kumamoto Castle, which dates from 1607.
