sources.text:
People missing in collapsed mall and factory after earthquake hits Japan
Nineteen people remain missing at a collapsed shopping centre and a damaged paper factory after a strong earthquake hit south-western Japan.
A local disaster management official told the BBC four people were rescued and another 10 are missing after a blast at the Aeon Mall in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, following the magnitude 6.8 tremor.
In Yatsushiro City, two people were found in a state of "cardiac arrest" and nine are unaccounted for after a chimney collapsed at Nippon Paper's Yatsushiro Plant.
The quake hit Kyushu island at 16:27 local time (07:27 GMT) on Tuesday, with hundreds of thousands of people told to move to evacuation shelters. A tsunami warning was lifted within one hour.
The quake was strong enough to be felt in South Korea.
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported it was a magnitude 7.1 tremor, which the US Geological Survey later measured as a 6.8. Quake magnitude figures are often updated as seismologists obtain and analyse new data.
The quake's shallow epicentre - with a depth of 10 km (six miles) - was about 20km south of Kumamoto city.
In nearby Kashima, the fire department said the Aeon shopping mall's "second floor collapsed".
Footage of the shopping centre shows white smoke rising from the building, as people run into the carpark. Large parts of the mall's exterior have been blown off, exposing the steel beams underneath.
An official from Kumamoto's disaster management division told the BBC the lives of the four rescued people at the mall were not in danger, but another 10 remained missing.
The official added that the prefecture was checking information about whether there had been a gas leak.
Aeon Mall is a popular nationwide chain that operates about 160 centres across Japan. It holds department stores, boutiques, pharmacies and food courts.
Elsewhere, footage aired by Japan's NHK broadcaster showed cracked roads and bridges and several buildings on fire. Train services were suspended and electricity cut off for thousands of homes.
NHK reported that dozens of people were injured during the earthquake. About 10 were in an elderly care home and at least 50 people were being treated in hospital.
"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said earlier in the day.
Felix Umland, a German photography student, was on the 13th floor of a hotel in Kagoshima, about 175km (109 miles) from the quake's epicentre.
"I just heard glasses flying in the kitchen and everything in the kitchen started breaking. There's not much you can do, it's a pretty hopeless situation. You're looking around waiting for it to stop," he told BBC's Newshour programme.
"In Japan the buildings are built to move with the earth but it feels like the building beneath you turns into liquid. It's a very surreal feeling. The solid ground just suddenly turned into a mass that was moving," Umland said.
The International Atomic Energy Agency posted to X that the earthquake "caused no damage or safety issues at the Sendai Nuclear Power Plant, located around 100km (62 miles) from the epicentre, and that it remains in operation".
"The IAEA will continue to monitor the situation," it said.
First responders have been deployed, including Japan's self-defence force, fire services and coast guard, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said.
"We urge residents in areas where the shaking was particularly severe to pay close attention to evacuation information issued by local authorities via radio, television and the internet, and to act calmly," he said.
Takaichi said 3,600 soldiers would be deployed to help with disaster recovery as tremors continued. Japan's Meteorological Agency has reported more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4.
Japan is one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries, experiencing about 1,500 quakes a year.
In 2016, 278 people were killed in a series of powerful earthquakes in Kumamoto, NHK reported at the time.

sources.news_title: Powerful 7.1-Magnitude Earthquake Rocks Southern Japan — Crisis Deepens After The Shaking Stops
sources.text:
Southern Japan was still counting the damage from a massive earthquake when a second emergency erupted.
The first shock struck the Kumamoto region late Tuesday afternoon, snapping roads, damaging buildings, starting fires and throwing parts of Kyushu into darkness.
Then, after the shaking had stopped and an evacuation was underway, an explosion tore through one of the prefecture’s largest shopping malls.
Rescue crews were searching the wreckage Tuesday night as workers remained unaccounted for and police warned that lives may have been lost.
NHK WORLD’s first aerial look showed just how widespread the emergency response had become:
The Japan Meteorological Agency placed the quake at 4:27 p.m. local time on July 28. Its epicenter was in the Kumamoto region at a shallow depth of roughly 10 kilometers, or about six miles.
JMA gave the earthquake a magnitude of 7.1 and recorded a maximum seismic intensity of 7 in Uki City and Hikawa Town. That is the highest point on Japan’s shindo scale, which measures the strength of shaking at a particular location rather than the total energy released by the quake.
Strong shaking spread well beyond the epicenter. Kumamoto’s southern ward registered an upper 6, while multiple communities across Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga and Miyazaki reached levels capable of causing major damage.
The agency issued a tsunami advisory for the Ariake and Yatsushiro Seas, then lifted it within two hours. No tsunami was observed from the inland quake.
The U.S. Geological Survey reviewed the same event at magnitude 6.8, centered about three miles east of Uto at a depth of 10 kilometers. JMA’s detailed mechanism page also lists a moment magnitude of 6.8 alongside its domestic magnitude of 7.1.
Those figures describe the quake through different measurement methods. They do not change what people on the ground experienced: the most severe level of shaking Japan’s intensity scale can record.
USGS placed the event on its highest alert tier for likely economic losses. Its current ShakeMap concentrates the strongest modeled shaking around Uto, Uki and the southern side of Kumamoto.
The reviewed location sits close to heavily populated communities and major transportation routes.
Japan’s government moved quickly from assessment to emergency response.
The Prime Minister’s Office of Japan said Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had received reports of injuries, power outages and fires, along with damaged roads and bridges and collapsed buildings. She said the government had created an emergency task force and was putting lives first.
Thousands of military personnel were being deployed to assist rescue operations while aircraft surveyed the hardest-hit areas. The government told agencies to collect damage information immediately, coordinate with local authorities and put rescue work ahead of everything else.
Authorities also warned residents to stay away from damaged structures and prepare for more strong shaking. Rail service across Kyushu was halted for inspections, flights were grounded and sections of highway cracked or shifted.
The earthquake itself was only part of the crisis.
Reuters reported that an explosion rocked Aeon Mall Kumamoto after customers and employees had begun evacuating following the initial quake. One side of the roughly 200-store complex was ripped open, exposing steel beams and scattering debris across the parking lot.
Fire officials said multiple people were trapped. NHK reported that roughly 20 to 30 workers were unaccounted for, while police told TBS that fatalities were feared.
The exact cause of the blast was still unknown. The explosion happened in the quake’s aftermath, but officials had not established that the earthquake directly caused it.
Hospitals were also treating scores of injured people. Reuters cited NHK reports that one hospital had received more than 50 patients and another about 40, including 10 people in serious condition.
Video from inside the region captured the violent side-to-side motion as it happened:
WATCH: Powerful shaking sends a building swaying side to side after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Kumamoto, Japan pic.twitter.com/NYeGx7ZCSS
— Insider Paper (@TheInsiderPaper) July 28, 2026
Kumamoto City reported that 181 shelters were open by 9 p.m. local time, housing 1,512 people from 858 households. Officials had ordered every city shelter opened as the damage assessment continued into the night.
Power was out at more than 47,000 homes across the prefecture at that hour. Parts of the city also lost gas and water service, while emergency crews responded to fires, people trapped in elevators and a road crack that forced a closure near the Midorikawa River.
The city applied Japan’s Disaster Relief Act across 21 municipalities because large numbers of people had been injured or faced an immediate threat to life and safety.
Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority reported no abnormalities at three nearby nuclear power plants, removing one of the most feared possibilities from the early damage picture.
Kumamoto knows how dangerous the next phase can be.
A devastating earthquake sequence struck the same region in 2016. The larger shock arrived after an earlier major quake, a history Japanese officials invoked as they warned people not to assume the danger had passed.
The first hours brought maximum-level shaking, widespread infrastructure damage, fires, blackouts, injuries and a mass evacuation.
What followed at the mall turned an already serious disaster into a race against time.
For the families waiting on word from rescue crews, the earthquake may have ended in seconds. The emergency did not.

sources.news_title: Mall collapses after powerful quake rocks Kumamoto
sources.text:
A powerful earthquake rocked Kumamoto Prefecture in the Kyushu region Tuesday, injuring scores and reportedly triggering an explosion that collapsed part of a shopping mall and left many people trapped.
The magnitude 7.1 quake registered up to a shindo 7, the highest level on the Japanese seismic intensity scale, and prompted multiple strong aftershocks. Authorities urged residents to remain vigilant for continued large quakes.
Local officials told NHK that the second floor of an Aeon shopping mall in the town of Kashima appeared to have collapsed, leaving a large number of people trapped following earlier reports of an explosion and white smoke rising from the building. Many fatalities are expected as a result of the collapse, a Kumamoto police source said, according to local broadcaster RKK.
NHK, quoting police sources, later reported between 20 and 30 employees at the mall were unable to be contacted, while four people — all conscious — had been transported from the mall to hospital.
Some 200 people had reportedly earlier evacuated to the mall’s parking lot.
Video showed portions of the mall’s exterior apparently blown off and steel beams exposed.
Meanwhile, at least 50 people had been injured and transported to hospital in the town of Hikawa, while more than 50 others were hospitalized in the city of Kumamoto, with at least one person unconscious, NHK said, citing local authorities.
Footage showed several collapsed buildings near the epicenter. The fire department in the city of Uki reported to the broadcaster that it had received many emergency calls as numerous fires broke out in the city.
Highway overpasses on the Kyushu Expressway in Yatsushiro sustained significant damage and what appeared to be the pedestrian portion of a bridge collapsed in the same city.
Operations on the entire length of the Kyushu Shinkansen line were suspended due to the quake, JR Kyushu said, while numerous local train lines also halted operations. The West Kyushu Shinkansen line was operating with delays.
According to West Nippon Expressway, the quake also prompted closures of expressways, mainly in Kumamoto Prefecture.
Speaking to reporters, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged those in the quake-hit areas “to remain vigilant for the possibility of another earthquake of similar magnitude,” adding that injuries from the disaster were likely to emerge.
“While we are still confirming the extent of damage, we have been informed that there are already injured people,” she said earlier without disclosing a figure.
Later, Takaichi announced the establishment of an emergency disaster task force, which she will head, and said that 3,600 Self-Defense Forces members will be dispatched for disaster relief operations at the request of the Kumamoto governor.
“I’d like to extend our heartfelt condolences and our thoughts are with those affected by this disaster,” she said.
“This is a very crucial moment and human lives come first.”
An official with the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) also urged people to remain on high alert for more earthquakes.
“Since there were strong quakes in this area in the past, which subsequently caused a series of strong temblors, please be on alert for up shindo 7 for around a week, especially for the next two to three days,” the official said during a news conference, referring to powerful quakes that struck the same area in 2016.
A quake with an epicenter over land at a shallow depth means seismic activity is active, which is likely to cause many aftershocks, he said.
The quake was caused after two faults slid horizontally in different directions, the official said. But he said it was too early to say whether the latest quake was related to the 2016 Kumamoto quakes. The epicenter of Tuesday’s quake was about 20 kilometers from the Hinagu fault zone, which caused the 2016 quake, the official said.
At a hastily organized news conference, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said that no abnormalities had been detected at the country’s nuclear power plants, including the Sendai facility in Satsumasendai, Kagoshima Prefecture.
The weather agency initially issued a tsunami advisory for coastal areas of the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas, urging people to stay away from the coast. All tsunami advisories were lifted at 6:10 p.m.
The rare shindo 7 was observed in Hikawa and the city of Uki. At that level, people cannot stay standing and may be thrown into the air, while unsecured pieces of furniture are likely to topple over or be tossed up in the air. Reinforced concrete walls may collapse.
This is the first quake that registered shindo 7 since the earthquake that struck the Noto Peninsula in January 2024.
A strong 6 on the shindo scale was observed in the cities of Yatsushiro, Uto and the towns of Mashiki and Misato, as well as the city of Kumamoto’s Minami Ward.
Shayne Bowden, 55, a researcher who resides in the area, was at the public library across from Kumamoto Station when the quake struck.
“I felt an initial jolt and then violent shaking, my laptop skidding across the desk back and forth,” he said.
People quickly got under the desks in the library and staff were calm while instructing people to evacuate.
“It kept shaking and shaking,” he said.
The Japan Times reached him while he was outside in a park as helicopters whirred overhead.
“The front of the station is full of people,” he said. “The konbini are packed, and there’s a bit of panic-buying.”
Other cities in Kumamoto, as well as the neighboring prefectures of Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga and Miyazaki, also felt strong shaking of a lower 5 or stronger on the Japanese scale.
The quake’s epicenter was in the city of Uki, just south of the city of Kumamoto, at a depth of 10 kilometers.
Electricity was out for about 48,300 households in Kumamoto Prefecture, according to Kyushu Electric. The company is asking people not to touch severed electricity lines, and notify them of any abnormalities.
The outages come as Japan is in the throes of a scorching summer, raising the prospects of a compound disaster. The JMA is forecasting highs of 34 degrees Celsius in Kumamoto for Wednesday, with highs projected to reach the upper 30s later in the week.
“We need to take precautions against heatstroke such as portable coolers,” Takaichi said.
The quake comes just over 10 years after two separate earthquakes rocked the city of Kumamoto in April 2016, leaving 278 people dead and injuring another 2,800.
Kumamoto Castle sustained heavy damage in the quakes and restoration work is not due to be completed until fiscal 2052.

U.S. & World
State broadcaster NHK carried footage of almost a dozen fire trucks in the facility’s parking lot. Images also showed the mall’s collapsed ceilings and facade and a debris-littered road.
Several other buildings were also damaged, video from the region showed. At least 12 houses collapsed, and at least 50 people were injured.
Aerial footage from NHK showed that a chimney at a Nippon Paper Industries plant in Yatsushiro, a city in the Kumamoto prefecture, had partially collapsed. Local police said that several people who work at the plant are unaccounted for.
“We are gathering information on whether there are any casualties, but we are concerned because we cannot reach them,” a spokesperson for the plant told NHK.
A verified video from the city showed that a rupture on the Kyushu Expressway had trapped vehicles. NHK showed aerial images of an elevated stretch of the highway where two sections had become misaligned.
Train services around the Kyushu island were suspended, rail operator JR Kyushu said.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a statement that 300 service members were being dispatched to the disaster zone.
“The government will spare no effort in emergency disaster response measures, with the highest priority placed on saving lives and rescue operations led by local police and fire departments,” her office said in a statement.
“Strong tremors, earthquakes of similar intensity may continue to occur over approximately the next week,” the statement added.
Japan experiences tremors — both minor and major — almost every day, making it one of the most earthquake-prone countries in the world. In 2016, Kumamoto was devastated by a series of quakes that killed nearly 300 people. The East Asian country sits on the “Ring of Fire,” where several tectonic plates converge, triggering many of the world’s earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
Nearly 20% of global earthquakes measuring 6.0 or higher occur in Japan. Since 2011, when a 9.0-magnitude earthquake and tsunami triggered meltdowns at three reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant and killed nearly 20,000 people, Japan has significantly strengthened its earthquake warning systems and evacuation protocols.
Japan’s nuclear authority informed the International Atomic Energy Agency that the Sendai nuclear power plant was not damaged in Tuesday’s earthquake, the IAEA said in a post on X.
Kyushu Electric Power said it had not found any abnormalities at either the Genkai Nuclear Power Station in Saga prefecture or the Sendai Nuclear Power Station in Kagoshima prefecture, NHK reported. The radiation levels around the stations have also not changed, it said.
Video published online and geolocated by NBC News appeared to show part of the outer walls of the Kumamoto Castle, a popular tourist destination in the area, damaged and surrounded by a cloud of dust.
An X account appearing to belong to the tourist attraction said that its operations would be suspended for at least the rest of Tuesday “due to the impact” of the earthquake.
Webcam video published online also appeared to show buildings shaking in Kumamoto city.

sources.news_title: Up to 30 trapped & many dead in Japan mall collapse after 7.1-mag quake
sources.text:
TWO women have been found dead after an explosion at a shopping centre in Japan triggered by a terrifying 7.1-magnitude earthquake.
At least 19 people are still missing in the wake of the disastrous tremor which has decimated neighbourhoods and ripped bridges apart.
The two deceased, both in their 20s, were discovered as rescue workers scoured the rubble of the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto for bodies following the quake.
During the tremor, the second floor of the shopping centre collapsed, trapping scores of customers and employees.
It was earlier reported that many people had died in the catastrophe, but authorities have only confirmed two deaths so far.
Several of the missing victims are believed to be mall employees.
Read more world news
Four people were previously rescued from Aeon Mall, and their lives are “not in danger”, authorities say.
But a further 10 people are still unaccounted for at the shopping centre.
Kashima Town, where the mall is located, is understood to have been hit by an aftershock with a magnitude of 5.
Police further said that around 200 people had taken refuge from the earthquake in the car park of the building when the explosion happened.
Most read in The US Sun
Additionally, two people “were found in cardiac arrest” and nine people are still missing at Nippon Paper’s Yatsushiro Plant.
The earthquake that shook Kumamoto on the southern island of Kyushu toppled buildings, sparked fires and injured more than 100.
Multiple people are also believed to be unaccounted for at a factory in Yatsushiro city where the tip of a chimney fell down, NHK reported.
One person was also killed when a house collapsed during the earthquake, Kyodo reported.
NHK aired footage from elsewhere in the southwestern Kumamoto region showing damaged bridges, a derailed cargo train and a number of houses threatening to topple over.
Footage showed dust clouds at famous Kumamoto Castle as stone walls appeared to collapse during the quake.
Other videos showed people ducking for cover inside a shopping centre as the building shook.
The Kyushu Expressway was also badly damaged by the earthquake, with two sections crumbled – with a large gap in between.
Chiharu Hara, a 35-year-old recruitment agent who was in Kumamoto, said she was “terrified” when the quake struck.
“The office swayed violently side-to-side. I was afraid it would collapse. Everyone panicked,” Hara said.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the government has received multiple reports of injuries, power outages and fires, as well as damage to roads, bridges and buildings.
Meanwhile, around 300,000 people have been urged to go to evacuation centres, and hundreds of soldiers have been deployed to help with rescue operations as aftershocks continued to rumble in the area.
Kyushu Electric Power said about 40,000 homes had lost power, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains.
Kumamoto airport also shut its runway, as airlines diverted and cancelled flights.
Japan‘s Meteorological Agency said the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, but the US Geological Survey revised it later to 6.8.
The earthquake happened at a depth of 6 miles below the sea surface and was followed by several more, some of which reached up to lower 5.
Warnings of waves of up to 3ft were issued, with Takaichi urging people to avoid the coastline. This was later cancelled.
Her government has set up a task force to gather information, assess possible damage and prepare for rescue operations if needed.
“We are putting people’s lives as the top priority,” the PM said, also urging residents in the strongly-shaken areas to use caution in light of possible strong aftershocks.
Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that killed more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.
Officials said there were no immediate abnormalities recorded at Japan’s nuclear power plants after the quake.
A quake with a magnitude of 7.2 hit northern Japan on June 25 but caused no deaths or major damage.
Japan is one of the world’s most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific “Ring of Fire”.
The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18 per cent of the world’s earthquakes.
The majority are mild, although the damage they cause varies according to their location and the depth below the Earth’s surface at which they strike.
In 2011, a huge 9.0-magnitude undersea quake triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.
On April 20 this year, a 7.7 tremor hit the country’s north, injuring at least 10 people and shaking large buildings in Tokyo.
It prompted authorities to issue a special advisory warning of an increased risk of earthquakes of magnitude 8.0 or stronger. The advisory was lifted after a week.

sources.news_title: What caused the magnitude 6.8 earthquake in Japan?
sources.text:
A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck just south of the city of Kumamoto on the southern Japanese island of Kyushu on Tuesday afternoon local time. The earthquake has ignited fires and damaged roads and buildings, including a mall where rescue workers are seeking to extract trapped people.
The earthquake occurred along a strike-slip fault, where the two sides of a fracture in Earth’s crust slide past each other, located in what independent earthquake scientist Amilcar Carrera-Cevallos calls “one of the most seismically complex spots in Japan.”
“Kyushu sits at a real tectonic crossroads,” he says. On one side, the Philippine Sea Plate is subducting under the Eurasian Plate at a rate of about 40 to 50 millimeters (1.6 to two inches) per year. But on the other side, there is also a so-called back-arc basin that is pulling apart. “That stretching reaches into central Kyushu and creates the Beppu-Shimabara graben, a rift zone riddled with active faults and volcanoes like Aso and Unzen,” Carrera-Cevallos says. “So you’ve got subduction pushing from one side and rifting pulling from the other, all crossed by a major strike-slip fault, the Median Tectonic Line.”
On supporting science journalism

The earthquake occurred in a local fracture inside the crust of the Eurasian Plate and was very shallow, at about 10 kilometers (six miles) below the surface. That shallowness “is a big part of why the shaking reached Shindo 7—the highest level on Japan’s scale—and why buildings and bridges collapsed,” Carrera-Cevallos says. It was also right under a population center, says Allen Husker, a California Institute of Technology geophysicist. If the quake had occurred closer to the subduction trench, the damage would’ve been less severe.
This earthquake happened along the same fault zone as a spate of deadly temblors in 2016. Those were also strike-slip earthquakes and hit some of the same towns. “The big difference is what happens next,” Carrera-Cevallos says. “In 2016 a smaller [magnitude] 6.2 earthquake struck first, and then, about a day and a half later, a much bigger [magnitude] 7.0 hit nearby on a different fault. Nobody expected that second, larger quake.”
Carrera-Cevallos says he is struck by how it did not take a strong subduction quake to create the highest level of shaking and cause substantial damage. This creates a difficult problem in structural engineering that aims to contend with seismological risk. Local faults “are numerous [and] poorly mapped compared to subduction interfaces, and they produce very high peak ground accelerations close to the source—exactly the kind of near-fault, high-frequency shaking that’s toughest on older, unreinforced structures,” he says. “This is a seismically mature, well-monitored region, but events like this remind us that even well-understood tectonic settings can still surprise us in their details.”
Additional reporting by Jackie Flynn Mogensen.

A violent earthquake of magnitude 7.1was registered in Japan southern, near the city of Kumamoto, on the island of Kyushu. There are numerous victims in the collapse of a shopping center, the Aeon Mall in Kashima, TBS television reported.
According to the broadcaster, a “considerable” number of people lost their lives due to the collapse of the second floor, perhaps caused by an explosion. The photos and videos released by NHK show an entire wing of the structure collapsed, with the external walls destroyed. Dozens of employees, between 20 and 30, are currently missing. Immediately after the earthquake, Mall staff helped customers evacuate but it is not clear how many managed to escape before an explosion caused the second floor of the department store to collapse.
In the early hours of the morning (Italian time) theJapanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had declared: “We are still assessing the extent of the injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries,” Takaichi said. “Power outages and fires are occurring in some areas, roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings have collapsed,” he further explained.
Some workers missing
One person died in a house collapse. This was reported by the Kyodo news agency. Some workers from a paper mill in the Kumamoto prefecture, the epicenter of the earthquake, are also missing.
The walls of Kumamoto Castle collapse
The earthquake also caused the collapse of part of the walls of the Kumamoto Castle. The Japanese media reported it. It is not the first time that the monument has been damaged by an earthquake: it had already happened in 2016 when a tremor measuring 7.3 degrees on the Richter scale caused the turrets and parts of the fortification to collapse. Long restoration works followed which were not yet completed. Kumamoto Castle is considered one of the three most important in Japan, along with Himeji and Matsumoto.
It was built between 1601 and 1607 by Kato Kiyomasa, a famous feudal lord of the time, who wanted to make it one of the most imposing and difficult fortresses in Japan to conquer thanks to the curved stones of the walls which would allow enemies to climb. And in fact the castle, where the emperor’s troops were barricaded, still resisted for weeks in 1877 the siege of the tens of thousands of rebel troops of Saigo Takamori, ‘the last samurai’, during the Satsuma revolt. After 50 days, the imperial army managed to overcome the rebels and Takamori was killed during the last battle on Mount Shiroyama. With him, the era of the samurai as a military aristocracy ended.
Tsunami warning lifted
The Japan Meteorological Agency has revoked the tsunami warning issued following the earthquake. The alert was removed from the agency’s website just under two hours after the tremor, recorded at 4.27pm local time (9.27am in Italy) on the island of Kyushu.
The quake was recorded at 4.27pm (09.27am in Italy) on the island of Kyushu.
No anomalies at nuclear sites
According to Japan’s Nuclear Regulatory Authority, no immediate anomalies were found at plants in the region. On Saturday, when Ukrainian drones hit military-supply lines connecting Russia and Iran through the Caspian Sea, thereby unofficially merging the Russo-Ukrainian War with the U.S.-Israeli War in Iran. Bill McGlaughlin, a composer, conductor, and long-time host of the classical radio show “Exploring Music,” died on 21 July at his home in the Upper West Side of New York. He was 82.
His partner, Karrin Allyson, confirmed his death, which she said was caused by cardiac arrest.
“It is with deep sorrow that I announce the passing of my beloved partner, Bill McGlaughlin,” Ms. Allyson wrote in a post on social media.
Mr. McGlaughlin – a multi-hyphenate who turned to music because his father had purchased a block of piano lessons for his younger brother, who then decided he had no interest in the instrument, leaving them to Bill, who was then 14 – decided he wanted to become a musician following his second piano lesson. It was at that point he began to practice eight hours a day. The piano was, however, his second instrument: the first was the harmonica. His father had given him one at the age of six and the two bonded over a love for opera and its melodies.
Today, Mr. McGlaughlin is being remembered as the original host of the popular daily one-hour classical music radio program, “Exploring Music,” which he hosted for over 23 years, from 2003 until his death. “Exploring Music,” like a university-level proseminar, covered a single over-arching topic each week such as composers inspired by paintings or poems, in which used performances by Alicia de Larrocha of “Goyescas,” by Enrique Granados, a musical transcription of Francisco Goya’s paintings, Mussorgsky’s “Pictures at an Exhibition,” and Hindemith’s “Mathis der Maler,” to illustrate the point. Several months ago, Mr. McGlaughlin put the spotlight on Artur Schnabel’s 1930s-era recordings of the 32 piano sonatas of Ludwig van Beethoven, where he contrasted Mr. Schnabel’s fiery, structurally fluid tempos with modern interpretations by pianists like Daniel Barenboim or Alfred Brendel.
In high school, Mr. McGlaughlin had taken up the trombone, which he continued to study after graduation at Temple University, where he obtained a Bachelor of Music degree in 1967. Upon graduation from Temple, he became assistant principal trombonist of the Philadelphia Orchestra, a position he held through 1968. From 1969 to 1975 he was co-principal trombonist of the Pittsburgh Symphony. His experiences with orchestral performance led to his interest in conducting, something that was encouraged by the conductor of the Pittsburgh, William Steinberg.

sources.text:
By AFP and published by CNA
TOKYO: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit Japan’s southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday (July 28), knocking out power to thousands of homes, rupturing roads and leaving some trapped and others reported dead inside a partially collapsed shopping mall.
In “Kashima town, a shopping complex’s second floor collapsed, leaving many people trapped inside”, the fire department said in a statement.
Broadcaster TBS said that a “considerable number” of people died in the shopping mall, though police told AFP they could not confirm whether there were any fatalities.
Fuji TV also reported that multiple deaths were confirmed at the Aeon Mall outlet in the Kumamoto region.
Speaking to reporters at her office in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago.
“We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” Takaichi said.
“I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.”
Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said, while Takaichi said 3,600 soldiers would be deployed to help with the disaster recovery as aftershocks continued to rumble.
“Like volcano ash was falling”
One hospital had reported more than 50 injuries, public broadcaster NHK said. Several people on a high-speed train at the time of the quake were also injured, media reported.
Multiple people were trapped inside an Aeon shopping mall rocked by an explosion that occurred after the earthquake, fire services said. Police said “quite a few” were presumed dead in the incident, broadcaster TBS reported.
An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear.
Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he heard the explosion while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall.
“It was a huge impact,” he said. “A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling.”
Buildings on fire
Several other buildings were also on fire or partially collapsed, according to footage from NHK, while large cracks appeared on major roads, including an elevated highway. Rail services were halted and flights grounded.
TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, evacuated workers from its plant in the area as a precaution, a spokesperson for the firm said.
Sony and Fujifilm also evacuated staff from their plants in the area, Nikkei newspaper reported. A Sony spokesperson earlier said it was checking the situation.
The quake’s epicentre was about 20km south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city with a population of around 700,000.
Residents in the areas that felt the biggest tremors must beware of further strong quakes for about a week, as well as the risk of landslides, an official for the Japan Meteorological Agency said.
Tsunami warning lifted
Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes.
Located along the “Ring of Fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20% of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more.
A tsunami warning was issued immediately after Tuesday’s quake, but was later lifted.
Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains.
Kumamoto airport also shut its runway, as airlines diverted and cancelled flights.
Telecoms operators KDDI and Docomo said there was disruption to their mobile phone services due to power shortages and transmission-line failures.
There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan’s nuclear regulation authority said.
A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739, based on an official count. It damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a top tourist site.
Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of Tuesday’s quake, an official at the castle’s office said.

sources.news_title: Explosion at mall in southwestern Japan leaves people trapped, injured after major earthquake
sources.text:
Tokyo, July 28 (SocialNews.XYZ) An explosion struck a large shopping centre in Kashima Town, Kumamoto Prefecture, on Tuesday, leaving multiple people trapped and injured, public broadcaster NHK reported.
According to Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency, information received from the local fire department indicated that part of Aeon Mall Kumamoto's second floor had collapsed, with numerous people believed to be trapped inside.
Firefighters were working to verify the situation and carry out rescue operations, the report said.
The agency also said that injured people had been transported to hospitals, although the number and severity of the injuries had not yet been disclosed, Xinhua News Agency reported.
Police and fire authorities said they received multiple emergency calls at around 6:00 p.m. local time reporting an explosion-like sound and white smoke rising from Aeon Mall Kumamoto.
Aerial footage filmed by an NHK helicopter at around 6:20 p.m. showed severe damage to the structure. Sections of the building's exterior wall had peeled away, exposing steel framework, while part of the roof appeared to have collapsed. A large hole was also visible on the rooftop.
The explosion occurred after a powerful earthquake of magnitude 7.1 struck Kumamoto Prefecture earlier in the day. According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, Kashima Town is believed to have experienced shaking of at least lower 5 on Japan's seismic intensity scale, although the exact intensity has yet to be confirmed.
The cause of the explosion remains under investigation.
The temblor occurred at around 4:27 p.m. local time at a depth of about 10 km, measuring a maximum of 7 on Japan's seismic intensity scale in the hardest-hit areas in the prefecture, the weather agency said.
A tsunami warning of one metre has been issued for the Ariake Sea and Yatsushiro Sea in southwestern Japan.

sources.text:
Several feared trapped in collapsed shopping mall after 7.1-magnitude earthquake in Japan
TOKYO —
Several people are trapped inside a shopping mall that partially collapsed in an explosion after a large 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck the Japanese city of Kumamoto on Tuesday, according to Japan’s public broadcaster NHK.
It is unclear how many people were trapped inside when the second floor of the building collapsed, NHK reported, citing fire officials. About 50 people were injured in the blast, NHK reported.
An aerial view shows the damaged Aeon Mall shopping centre after an explosion following an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 that struck Japan’s southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday.
The earthquake struck the city of Kumamoto, about 55 miles east of Nagasaki in southern Japan, on Tuesday afternoon local time, causing a highway bridge to buckle and at least one other building to collapse.
In their initial estimate, local police said nine people were unaccounted for, but Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi stressed to reporters the number of casualties and extent of the damage was unclear and still being assessed, Reuters reported.
“We have already been informed that people have been injured,” Takaichi said. “Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings.”
Chipmaker TSMC evacuated workers from its plant in the area as a precaution, a spokesperson for the firm told Reuters.
Kyodo News agency said a hospital in Yatsushiro city accepted about 40 people with injuries from the quake. A train was derailed and fell on its side at the Yatsushiro station, and stone walls were damaged at the Kumamoto castle, Kyodo said.
Yozo Kai, a priest at a Shinto shrine in the nearby town of Mashiki, said a few stone lanterns fell down. “I worried if the main hall and the gate would tilt again,” he told Kyodo.
A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured 2,739 more.
“The shaking reminded me of the Kumamoto quake (10 years ago) and I was frightened,” said Hiroki Shimoda, an official at the Mifune town hall, who saw rooftiles of nearby homes crash down to the ground.
Japan’s Fire and Disaster Management Agency said there were no reports of damage to major public facilities and infrastructure, though authorities were still assessing the extent of damage. Local fire departments received many emergency calls reporting fires and damage to homes.
“We are putting people’s lives as the top priority,” Takaichi said, urging residents in the strongly shaken areas to use caution in light of possible aftershocks.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Many feared dead in Japanese mall after quake
sources.text:
Japanese broadcaster TBS reported that a "considerable number" of people have died in a shopping mall in the southwestern city of Kumamoto, which was damaged by a major earthquake on Tuesday.
Other Japanese media said the casualties happened after an explosion at the Aeon Mall.
Emergency services earlier said "many people" were trapped inside the building after a floor collapsed. 
The Aeon Mall had just reopened last month as a new and improved shopping and entertainment complex to commemorate its recovery from a deadly tremor a decade ago.
The mall was so badly damaged in the magnitude 7.3 Kumamoto earthquake in April 2016 that it had to close for months and rebuild over even longer periods. As it went through a 2017 redevelopment and expansion, the mall highlighted its seismically reinforced ceilings and overall improvements to safety and resilience.
On Tuesday, much of the sprawling site was reduced to a skeleton and rubble. 
Kumamoto police said the danger of aftershocks made it impossible to start search and rescue work in the compromised structure. 
The epicentre of the quake was only a few miles away.
When the magnitude 7.1 tremor struck late afternoon on Tuesday, mall employees helped evacuate visitors outside the building, an Aeon spokesperson said. 
About 200 people had been guided outside to safety, prefectural authorities said.
About an hour later, a powerful explosion blew the walls off and exposed large parts of the underlying structure. 
Some 20 to 30 employees at the mall were still unaccounted for, public broadcaster NHK said. 
Witnesses reported smelling gas in the area. (Agencies)

sources.news_title: Japan struck by M6.8 earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture. Damage reported limited so far - Artemis.bm
sources.text:
An earthquake has struck Japan in the Kumamoto prefecture of Kyushu. Preliminarily given a 7.1 magnitude, this has now been revised down to M6.8 by the USGS. However, Japan’s earthquake scale reports shaking at Shindo 7 level from this relatively shallow event, which is likely to result in some damage although reports are limited so soon after the event.
The earthquake struck just south of Kumamoto city in the last hour and was at a depth of about 10 kilometers, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. That is relatively shallow and quakes can cause greater shaking effects when closer to the surface.
The Japanese Shindo earthquake scale has reported level 7 shaking in some areas, which is at the highest on the scale.
A Shindo 6 level of shaking was reported for urban areas such as the cities of Yatsuhiro and Uto, as well as the towns of Mashiki and Misato, and even in the city of Kumamoto’s Minami Ward, according to Japanese media reports.
A a tsunami advisory has been issued for areas of the Ariake and Yatsushiro coasts, although no reports of any major impacts have been seen at this time.
Other areas of Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga and Miyazaki prefectures have all experienced Shindo 5 level shaking, reports state.
Kyushu Electric reported around 48,000 households are without power after the earthquake.
CNN has reported that firms including Sony and TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, have plants in the area of the quake, but so far there are no reports of damage.
An earthquake a decade ago near Kumamoto that struck at magnitude 7.0 was estimated to have caused insurance and reinsurance market losses of up to US $4 billion, currency converted at the time.
Japan remains a peak peril zone for its earthquake and typhoon exposure, with meaningful insurance limit and global reinsurance capacity exposed to major events there.
Japan is also a peak peril zone for the catastrophe bond market.
There is currently $1.55 billion of outstanding cat bonds that are solely exposed to Japanese earthquake risks, while there is more exposure held in Japanese multi-peril deals ($100m definitely has exposure to earthquake events) and international multi-peril cat bond structures.
The catastrophe bonds exposed to Japanese earthquakes would typically be expected to be more exposed to more intense quakes than this. However with much of that coverage being indemnity triggered, there can always be a some uncertainty, or a potential threat, if damage turns out to be meaningful (at this time that is not the case, damage reports are limited at this time).
It’s worth also noting that much of the Japanese cat bond exposure is based on residential property damages, rather than commercial.
There is also likely to be parametric insurance covers in the region, given it has quite a large industrial base and some significant cities and urban areas. Again though, most parametric triggers are likely to be set for earthquakes at higher intensity than magnitude 7, although some could be based on the levels of ground shaking seen.
It’s too early at this time to have a clear picture of the scale of any damage from today’s earthquake and with aftershocks still occurring, there has been an M5.6 and M4.9 so far, the insurance, reinsurance and cat bond markets will need to watch developments with this event closely until clarity of the impact of this event emerges.
We will update this story, or report again, if damage reports suggest a greater threat to any structures.
Updates:
Media reports have shown property damage in parts of the prefecture and Kumamoto city itself. Damage to commercial and residential buildings is being reported, as well as to some industrial structures and the main Kumamoto expressway road.
A second floor has collapsed in the Aeon shopping mall in Kumamoto city, with an unspecified number of people trapped and rescuers now attempting to free them. Sadly, Japanese media is reporting there are likely to have been some deaths from this structural damage.
Damage is also being investigated and a number of people are reported missing after the Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant, located in Yatsushiro City, was impacted by the quake.
Still, damage appears less widespread than in previous large Japanese earthquake events, such as the Noto Peninsula event in 2024. Although cumulatively the loss to insurance companies may prove to be among the more significant disaster events of recent years, it now seems. It remains too early to know whether there will be any impact to reinsurance arrangements.

Japan rocked by several earthquakes, including magnitude 6.8 quake, as Pacific Ring of Fire activity continues
Japan sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a 25,000-mile belt of volcanoes and earthquake zones surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean.
KUMAMOTO, Japan — A series of earthquakes rocked Kyushu, Japan's southernmost main island Tuesday afternoon, including a magnitude 6.8 earthquake that struck roughly 9 miles north of the city of Kumamoto.
Nearly a dozen fires broke out and a building partially collapsed following the earthquakes, triggering hundreds of emergency calls.
The main earthquake struck just before 4:30 p.m. local time and was relatively shallow, with an epicenter about 6 miles beneath the surface. It was felt across much of Kyushu, according to the USGS.
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) issued a tsunami advisory for parts of Kyushu, warning of waves up to 3 feet, before lifting it a short time later.
A magnitude 5.6 and a magnitude 4.9 earthquake struck near the city of Tsunagi within an hour of the main earthquake. A magnitude 4.4 quake struck just east of Uki shortly after 7 p.m.
